output.content:
The street had moved overnight.

I know that because I drew it.

I drew it yesterday afternoon, with a ruling pen and a field book still damp from the rain, and I drew it again this morning, and between the two drawings Hutum Pukur Lane had shifted twelve yards to the east and turned its shoulder a little toward the river.

I was sitting at the table I had built myself from teak and cast-off Survey office plans, lamp oil gone low, the window over the courtyard at Bowbazar open to the wet heat that came off the Hooghly after a monsoon. The map of Ward Seven lay on the table beside my tea, which had gone cold. The ink on it was still bright, the line of Hutum Pukur Lane a clean black spine between two smaller veins of houses. The field book lay open to the 28th of August.

It was there in the book. Chain length 73.4 yards from the corner of Nimtola Ghat to the first neem tree. Bearing 82 degrees. No error.

Bansi, who brought my lamp oil and kept the kerosene from the street dogs, leaned over my shoulder in his bare feet.

“Again?” he asked.

He was sixteen and could read Bengali better than I could, because he had not been trained at the Survey Office to write only in English.

“It is the same lane,” I said. “It should be.”

He pointed, because he had been watching me check this map for three weeks. “Yesterday it finished at the well.”

“There is no well anymore.”

He shrugged. “Yesterday there was.”

That was the whole problem. I had not been imagining it.

My name is Meera Sen. I am twenty-nine, a draughtswoman in the Trigonometrical Survey under Mr. Whitby, who signs my pay slips and tells the men in the bullock carts to give me room. I am not allowed the title of surveyor. I am allowed the pen. I measure with a chain left by the men, and I ink what they bring back, and I make the city legible for the men who will never live in it.

I had been given Ward Seven because it was tangled. The new tram line had cut through, the old lanes had been renamed after the cholera, and no one in the Survey had a complete sheet since 1878. They wanted it clean by December for the Darjeeling map fair.

I had been working from a rooftop on the west side of the street, dropping the chain down to Bansi to hold, and for three days the lane had been steady. The houses on the north side were the widow’s quarter, the houses on the south were the oil presses. Hutum Pukur Lane ended at a locked compound wall with a white bull carved into it.

This morning Hutum Pukur Lane ended at a different wall. It ended, in fact, just in front of the small tea stall where I bought my morning luchi, a stall that according to every previous sheet was on Akra Street.

I checked the field book. I checked the chain marks I had burned into the eaves of the neem tree. I checked the brass button I had placed at the corner as a reference. The button was where it should be. The lane was not.

“Perhaps the rain moved the paper,” Whitby said when I showed him the overlay at noon.

He was a thin man with a moustache like a brush and a habit of tapping his pencil on the desk when he was annoyed. He had a map of Burma pinned to his wall and a cup of tea he never drank.

“The paper is on linen,” I said.

“It is humid.”

“The line has moved twelve yards.”

“Then you drew it wrong yesterday.”

He tapped his pencil. “Miss Sen, in the Survey we do not chase ghosts. We make the map true. The city is not moving.”

I pressed the two sheets together, one from the 27th, one from the 28th. The street jumped like a fish.

“Would you like me to walk it again?” I asked.

He sighed. “Do what you must. But do not waste the office’s ink.”

I walked it again at three in the afternoon. The monsoon had lifted enough for the sun to cut white lines through the mist. The lane was where the Survey said it should be. The tea stall was on Akra Street. The bull wall was at the end of Hutum Pukur Lane. Children played hopscotch in the dust. An old woman sold paan from a tin. No one noticed me with the chain.

I checked the brass button. I checked the neem tree. I checked the wall.

Everything was correct.

At midnight I locked the shutters and lit the lamp again. I had not intended to work that late, but the air was cool and the city sounded different after dark, like a different city. I took out the fresh linen sheet I had prepared for Ward Seven and pricked the holes for the north line.

Bansi had left a clay cup of tea. I drank it. I inked the lane from the button outward, following my notes exactly. The line lay clean and true.

I blew out the lamp at one, with the sheet under the weight stone.

The next morning, the sheet was wrong.

The lane had moved again. Not twelve yards this time. Eight. It had shifted south, toward the presses, and its end now touched the tea stall. The tea stall, which the day before had been perfectly on Akra Street, now sat inside Hutum Pukur Lane.

I did not go to Whitby. I went to the lane.

I walked it with the chain and my notebook and Bansi beside me with a lantern because the rain had started again. The lane was exactly as it had been. The tea stall was on Akra Street. The lane ended at the bull wall.

I stood still until the rain soaked through my cotton sari.

That night I did not wait for morning. I waited for dark and then I went out again, alone, with a lantern and the map folded under my arm.

The streets after midnight in Bowbazar were not for women who carried measuring chains. The dogs knew me and let me pass. The tram had stopped running. The river smelled of fish and mud.

I found Hutum Pukur Lane. I stood at the button and opened the map to the fresh linen. I held the lantern low so the light fell on the paper.

The lane on the map was there, inked, true. Then, as I watched, the line seemed to breathe. I know that sounds like fever. It was not fever. The ink looked wet. The line trembled at the edge where I had lifted the pen.

I stepped back. The lantern caught the wet paper and the line looked like a road in a puddle.

A sound came from the lane. Not dogs. A humming, low and tuneless, like a woman singing while she worked. I followed it because the chain in my hand told me the bearing was wrong.

The humming led me to the bull wall. The wall had a door I had never recorded. It was a narrow wooden door set into the compound, half-eaten by termites, with a brass handle green with age. No one had ever told me it was there.

I lifted the lantern. The door was shut. The humming was on the other side.

I pressed my palm to the wood. It was warm.

I pulled the map from under my arm and pressed it against the door. The ink of Hutum Pukur Lane lined up perfectly with the doorframe on the map, as if the lane had been drawn to end there all along, and the paper had simply been waiting for the door to admit it.

The humming stopped. A bolt slid back inside the wall. The door opened a fraction, just enough for a sliver of light to spill out, and the light fell on the paper in my hand. The ink there darkened.

Then the light changed. The paper was wet. The line of Hutum Pukur Lane moved.

I saw it shift on the linen under my fingers, stretching toward the open door, inch by inch, as if it were being pulled by a hand I could not see. The paper, which had been dry and cool, was now damp, as if it had been raining on it for a long time.

The door opened wider.

I should have run. I should have closed the map and gone home. Instead I stepped through the sliver of light.

The air inside was warm and smelled of old ink and turmeric. The lane was there inside, not a street but a corridor of paper walls, and at the far end, under a lamp that burned with a steady flame, a woman sat at a table identical to mine, drawing with a ruling pen.

She looked up. She was older than me, maybe fifty, her hair in a tight braid, her sari the color of monsoon. She had my face.

“Finally,” she said, and she did not sound surprised. She had a map open in front of her, and on the map, Ward Seven was complete, every lane inked in, and the line of Hutum Pukur Lane led straight to the courtyard of my own house in Bowbazar, where my table sat.

“You have been moving it home,” she said.

Outside, the river kept moving, and the monsoon kept falling.

I tried to speak. My throat was full of ink.

She pointed to the paper in my hand. “Do not finish it. If you finish it, it will be true.”

Then the door behind me shut. The bolt slid home.

I was standing in the lane again, lantern in hand, map damp and heavy. The door was a plain compound wall with no handle, no door at all. The bull carving stared back at me.

I walked home fast, the chain clinking against my leg. When I got to my courtyard I unlocked the shutter and laid the map on the table, under the weight stone.

The line of Hutum Pukur Lane was no longer where I had drawn it. It had moved again, but not eight yards or twelve. It had moved straight, a clean unbroken line from the river, through the city, past Whitby’s office, past the Survey, past the tram lines, and it ended at the edge of my own paper, at the very spot where my lamp sat.

On the back of the linen, in a hand that was not mine but was mine, a new street name had appeared, written in faint charcoal as if from the other side.

It read: Meera Sen Lane.
